At advanced level, the hard part of Excel is rarely the formula. It is the **shape of the data**. Many business workbooks in Nigeria look neat on screen but are built like a paper notebook: one block per month side by side, merged headings, a "Total" row every few lines, and amounts typed as text such as "N45,000". A person can read that. Excel cannot summarise it reliably. In this lesson you learn the layout that every PivotTable, lookup and dashboard in this course depends on.

Clean, one-row-per-record tables are the foundation of every automated report in this course.
The rules of tidy data
**One row = one record.** One sale, one payment, one delivery. Never a mix of records and subtotals.
**One column = one kind of information.** Date in one column, customer in another, quantity in another. Do not write "12 bags @ 14,500" in a single cell.
**One header row, unique names, no merged cells.** Merged cells break sorting, filtering and copying formulas down.
**No blank rows or blank columns inside the data.** Excel treats a blank row as the end of the list.
**Numbers stored as numbers, dates stored as dates.** Type 45000 and format it as currency; do not type the naira sign or the word "naira" into the cell.
**Months as values, not as separate blocks.** A Month column (or a real Date column) replaces twelve side-by-side tables.

A quick test for numbers: select a column of amounts and look at the status bar at the bottom of the Excel window. If it shows **Sum**, the values are numbers. If it only shows **Count**, they are text, usually because of a leading apostrophe, a typed currency sign or spaces copied from another system. Text numbers silently drop out of totals, which is one of the most common causes of a report that is "a little bit off".
Excel Tables: the single most useful habit

Once the data is tidy, click any cell inside it and press **Ctrl+T** (or Insert > Table), confirm that "My table has headers" is ticked, and click OK. Your range is now an **Excel Table**. Go to the Table Design tab and give it a meaningful name in the Table Name box, for example **tblSales**. Professionals name every table, because names make formulas readable and make PivotTables find the data automatically.

Three layers: data, calculations, dashboard

Advanced workbooks keep different jobs on different sheets. The **Data** sheets hold raw Tables and nothing else. A **Calc** sheet (some people call it Workings) holds PivotTables, helper formulas and lookup lists. The **Dashboard** sheet only shows results: headline numbers, charts and slicers. The person who types sales never needs to touch the dashboard, and the person who reads the dashboard never sees a raw formula. This also makes checking much easier, because every number on the dashboard can be traced back one step at a time.

SUMIFS, COUNTIFS and AVERAGEIFS

The pattern is: what to add up first, then pairs of where to look and what to look for. **=SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, criteria_range2, criteria2, ...)**. Note that the older SUMIF puts the sum range last, while SUMIFS puts it first. Mixing them up is a classic error. COUNTIFS has no sum range, only pairs of conditions. AVERAGEIFS follows the SUMIFS order.

For dates, put the start and end dates in cells and join them to a comparison sign with the **&** symbol. If H1 holds 01/03/2025 and H2 holds 31/03/2025, the March condition is two pairs: tblSales[Date], ">="&H1 and tblSales[Date], "<="&H2. Never type the date inside the quotes, because a different computer may read 03/04 as 3 April or 4 March depending on its regional settings.
Worked example: March layer mash sales in Oyo
For example, Tola wants one dashboard cell showing layer mash sales to customers in Oyo during March. Her settings are in cells: H1 = 01/03/2025, H2 = 31/03/2025, H3 = Layer mash, H4 = Oyo.
She writes =SUMIFS(tblSales[Amount], tblSales[Product], H3, tblSales[Town], H4, tblSales[Date], ">="&H1, tblSales[Date], "<="&H2).
To test it, she filters tblSales by Product = Layer mash, Town = Oyo and March dates. Five rows remain: 174,000; 290,000; 145,000; 87,000; 232,000.
The SUMIFS cell shows 928,000, so the formula is right. She copies the same structure with COUNTIFS to show 5 invoices, and divides to get an average invoice of 928,000 / 5 = 185,600.
Changing H3 to Broiler starter or H4 to Ogbomoso now updates the answer instantly, which is exactly how dashboard selectors will work later.
XLOOKUP: exact matches, missing items and tiers

**=XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode])**. The first three arguments do the basic job: find this value in this column and bring back the matching item from that column. To fetch a product's price from a Table called tblProducts: =XLOOKUP([@Product], tblProducts[Product], tblProducts[Price]). The fourth argument lets you show a clear message instead of #N/A, for example "Not in price list".

The fifth argument, match_mode, is what makes tiered rates easy. **0** is exact match (the default). **-1** means exact match, or if none is found, the next smaller item. **1** means the next larger item. **2** allows wildcards such as * and ?. Microsoft states that XLOOKUP is not available in Excel 2016 and Excel 2019, so check the client's version first.

With that tier table in tblTiers, a sales rep with 760,000 naira of sales gets =XLOOKUP(760000, tblTiers[From], tblTiers[Rate], , -1). There is no exact 760,000 row, so match_mode -1 returns the next smaller tier, 500,000, which pays 3%. Commission is 760,000 x 3% = 22,800 naira. INDEX and MATCH for older versions and two-way lookups

If the client uses Excel 2016 or 2019, combine **INDEX** (return the item at a row and column position) with **MATCH** (find the position of a value). For a target grid with products down column A and months across row 1, =INDEX(B2:M6, MATCH(H3, A2:A6, 0), MATCH(H5, B1:M1, 0)) returns the target for the product in H3 and the month in H5. The 0 in MATCH means exact match. This two-way pattern works in every version of Excel.

Calculated fields and their trap

Under PivotTable Analyze > Fields, Items & Sets > Calculated Field, you can create a field such as Margin = Profit / Amount. A calculated field always works on the **sums** of its fields, not row by row. For a margin percentage that is exactly what you want: total profit divided by total sales. But a field like Bags * Price would multiply total bags by total prices, which is meaningless. Calculate row-level amounts in the Table first, then let the pivot add them up.
Refreshing and GETPIVOTDATA

PivotTables do **not** update by themselves when data changes. Use **Data > Refresh All** after adding data; it refreshes every pivot and query in the workbook. You can also tick "Refresh data when opening the file" in PivotTable Options > Data. When you click a pivot cell while writing a formula elsewhere, Excel inserts a GETPIVOTDATA formula. It is useful for dashboard cards because it keeps pointing at the right item even when the pivot changes size. If you want a plain cell reference instead, untick Generate GetPivotData in the PivotTable Analyze > Options drop-down.
One Table, many pivots
Pivots made from the same Table share a pivot cache, which keeps the file smaller and allows one slicer to control several pivots at once. You will use this in Module 2.

Most dashboards are fed by exports: a CSV from a point-of-sale (POS) system, a statement downloaded from a bank or payment platform, a report from accounting software. Each month someone opens the file, deletes the junk rows at the top, fixes the dates, and pastes it under last month's data. This is slow and it is where errors creep in. **Power Query**, found on the Data tab under **Get & Transform Data**, records those cleaning steps once and repeats them every time you refresh.

How Power Query thinks

Power Query opens its own window, the **Power Query Editor**. Every action you take, such as removing rows or changing a column type, is added to a list called **Applied Steps** on the right. Nothing in your original file is changed. When you click Close & Load, the cleaned result is loaded into a new Excel Table. Next month, Refresh All runs the same steps on the new data. You can click any step to see the data at that stage, or delete a step that was wrong.

KPI cards that calculate correctly

A KPI card is a few merged-looking cells (use Center Across Selection rather than Merge) showing a label, a big number and a comparison. Feed the number from GETPIVOTDATA or SUMIFS on the Calc sheet. Percentage change is **(this period - last period) / last period**. Margin is **gross profit / sales**, calculated from totals, never by averaging the margins of individual items.

Select a PivotTable and choose PivotTable Analyze > PivotChart. Dynamic arrays for live lists

In Excel 2021, 2024 and Microsoft 365, some functions return many results that **spill** into the cells below. =SORT(UNIQUE(tblSales[Branch])) produces a clean branch list for a drop-down. =FILTER(tblDebtors, (tblDebtors[Status]="Unpaid")*(tblDebtors[Days]>30), "No overdue accounts") lists every unpaid account over 30 days. The * means AND; a + would mean OR. Without the third argument, an empty result shows #CALC!. If something is in the way of the spill, you get #SPILL!, so leave the cells below a spilling formula empty.

A wrong number that looks right is worse than an obvious error, because people act on it. Before a dashboard is handed over, you need proof that it reconciles with the source, that it survives normal mistakes by users, and that someone other than you can keep it running. Professional Excel builders treat this as part of the job, and it is often what clients remember.

Control totals and check cells

Create a small Checks area on the Calc sheet. Each check compares two numbers that must agree and shows the difference. For example, =SUM(tblSales[Amount]) - GETPIVOTDATA("Sales", Pivots!$A$3) should be 0. =ROWS(tblSales) should equal the row count in the POS reports. Add conditional formatting so any non-zero difference turns red, and place one summary cell on the dashboard, for example =IF(COUNTIF(Checks!C2:C8,"<>0")=0, "All checks OK", "Check data").
Worked example: the 312,500 naira gap
For example, Ada's check cell shows the dashboard sales total is 18,600,000 while the source Table adds up to 18,912,500.
The difference is 18,912,500 - 18,600,000 = 312,500 naira, so something is missing from the pivot.
She clicks the pivot and opens PivotTable Analyze > Change Data Source. It points to a fixed range, Data!$A$1:$H$6200, created before the data was a Table.
She filters the Table for rows below row 6200 and finds 5 late invoices of 62,500 each. 5 x 62,500 = 312,500, which explains the whole gap.
She changes the data source to tblSales, clicks Refresh All, and the check cell returns 0.
The fix is permanent: because the pivot now reads the Table, future rows are always included.
Finding the cause of a wrong number
**Trace Precedents** (Formulas tab) draws arrows to the cells a formula uses. Trace Dependents shows what relies on a cell.
**Evaluate Formula** steps through a formula one part at a time, which shows exactly where a SUMIFS condition fails.
**Show Formulas** (Ctrl+` , the key above Tab) displays formulas instead of results, making inconsistent formulas easy to spot.
**Error checking:** a green triangle in a cell often means a number stored as text or a formula that differs from its neighbours.
Test with awkward data on purpose

Real users make mistakes, so test like one. On a copy of the file, add rows that break the usual pattern: a blank quantity, a zero amount, a date typed as text, a date in the future, a duplicate invoice number, and a branch or product name that is not in your lists. Then refresh and watch the Checks area and the dashboard. Each problem should either be blocked by data validation or be caught by a check cell. A duplicate invoice can be flagged with a helper column such as =COUNTIFS(tblSales[Invoice],[@Invoice])>1, which shows TRUE for repeats. Write down what you tested and what happened; that list becomes part of your handover notes and shows the client the tool was properly tested.
Do not hide errors with IFERROR

Wrapping everything in IFERROR(..., 0) makes a broken lookup look like a real zero. Use XLOOKUP's if_not_found argument with a clear message such as "Not in price list", or let the error show while testing so you can fix the cause.
Protecting the workbook from accidents
Add **data validation** to input cells: Data > Data Validation, for example a List of branches from the UNIQUE list, or whole numbers greater than 0 for quantities.
Every cell is Locked by default. Select only the input cells, press Ctrl+1, open the Protection tab and untick Locked.
Review > Protect Sheet. Allow "Select unlocked cells" and, on dashboard sheets, "Use PivotTable & PivotChart". Then test that the slicers and timeline still work.
Review > Protect Workbook (structure) stops users deleting or renaming sheets.
Protection is not security

Sheet protection prevents accidental changes; it does not keep confidential data private, and protection passwords can be removed with freely available tools. For files containing salaries, customer details or bank information, use File > Info > Protect Workbook > Encrypt with Password, use a strong password, and share it through a different channel from the file.

Data protection

Business data often includes personal data: customers' names, phone numbers, pupils' records, staff salaries. Nigeria's **Data Protection Act 2023**, overseen by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), sets rules for how personal data is collected and processed. In practice for you: ask only for the fields the dashboard needs, ask the client to remove or replace names where possible, agree in writing how files will be shared (a business cloud folder rather than personal WhatsApp), and delete your copies when the project ends.
Worked example: discovery with a school bursar

For example, Mrs Bello is bursar of a private primary school in Abuja with 420 pupils. She currently tracks fees in a large sheet with one tab per class and spends most of each Friday answering the proprietor's questions about who has paid.

Data: payments arrive by bank transfer and are typed in by the bursar. Fee amounts per class sit in a separate price list. That means one payments Table, one pupils Table and one fee Table.

Privacy: pupil names stay on the school's computer. The builder works on a copy where names are replaced with pupil ID numbers.
Success measure agreed: the Friday report should take under 15 minutes instead of most of a day.

Working out your hourly rate

Start from what you need to earn, not from what you think others charge. Decide a monthly income target, then estimate how many hours a month you can actually bill. Billable hours are always fewer than working hours, because finding clients, learning, admin and unpaid revisions also take time. For example, if your target is 400,000 naira a month and you expect about 50 billable hours, your minimum rate is 400,000 / 50 = 8,000 naira per hour. Then compare with what similar freelancers and training providers in your area charge, and with the value to the client. As your portfolio grows and your estimates prove accurate, raise your rate for new clients first.

Break the work into phases and estimate each one. Add a contingency, often 15 to 25 percent, for unknowns such as messier data than expected. Track your actual hours on every project in a simple sheet; after three or four projects your estimates will become much more accurate, because they will be based on your own record.

At advanced level, the hard part of Excel is rarely the formula. It is the shape of the data. Many workbooks look neat on screen but are built like a paper notebook.
In this module you turn messy lists into proper Excel Tables, then write formulas that answer questions like: sales of layer mash, in Oyo, in March.

Tidy data
One row = one record, no subtotal rows
One column = one kind of information
One header row, no merged cells
No blank rows or columns inside the data
Numbers as numbers, dates as dates
One row is one record: one sale, one payment. Never mix records with subtotals.
One column holds one kind of information. Do not write 12 bags at 14,500 in a single cell.
Use one header row with unique names. Merged cells break sorting, filtering and copying formulas.
Excel treats a blank row as the end of the list.

And type 45000, not the naira sign. Here is a quick test. Select the amounts and look at the status bar. If it shows Sum, they are numbers. If it only shows Count, they are text, and they silently drop out of your totals.

Turn a list into a named Table

Tola runs a poultry feed business in Ibadan. She copies each sale into its own row, clicks inside the list and presses Control T.

She adds an Amount column: Bags on this row times Price per bag on this row. Excel fills it down the whole column at once.
Then she checks by hand. 12 times 14,500 is 174,000. 8 times 15,200 is 121,600.
Keep colours and notes for the dashboard. A single blank row or subtotal inside the data distorts every total built on it.

Lookups
Points at the return column
VLOOKUP without its last argument uses approximate match. On an unsorted list it can return a wrong price with no error at all. Always end it with FALSE.
XLOOKUP is safer, and its match mode minus 1 handles tiers. A rep with 760,000 naira of sales gets the 500,000 tier at 3 percent, so 22,800 naira commission.
XLOOKUP needs Excel 2021, 2024 or Microsoft 365. For 2016 or 2019, use INDEX with MATCH.

Add Amount as a plain sum, then as percent of grand total, then as percent difference from the previous month. In one example, layer mash was 50 percent of sales, and March grew by 19.6 percent.

Questions that shape the job
What decisions should this report help with?
How is the report made now, and how long?
Where does the data come from, how often?

A discovery call usually takes 30 to 60 minutes. Start from the decisions the owner makes each week or month.
Ask how the report is made now and how long it takes. That time saved supports your price.
Ask where the data comes from, and ask to see a sample of it, even ten rows with names removed.

At the school, pupil names stay on the school's computer. The builder works on a copy with names replaced by pupil ID numbers.
Agree in writing how files are shared. A business cloud folder, not personal WhatsApp.
